summary:
We developed SPATIAL COMPATIBILITY, an interactive web application that functions as a global search engine and parametric characterization tool for spatial analogs.
To address this challenge in an innovative way, the platform goes beyond simple visual comparison by utilizing geocoding and open data (weather APIs and historical telemetry from NASA). When any location on Earth is entered, the algorithm cross-references its real-world climate data with the extreme conditions of the lunar South Pole and Mars. This generates an automated technical matrix that highlights the terrain’s operational advantages and warns of insurmountable physical limitations, such as microgravity and radiation.
This project is important because it democratizes space science: it allows any researcher to parametrically validate unexplored local locations—such as glaciovolcanic fields—as viable laboratories for testing rovers, spacesuits, and ISRU technologies, thereby mitigating risks ahead of the Artemis missions.
details:
SPACE COMPATIBILITY is an interactive web application that democratizes the search for space test sites. Rather than relying solely on visual similarities, our tool uses geocoding, open-source terrestrial climate data, and real NASA telemetry to parametrically compare any location on Earth with conditions on the Moon and Mars. The platform generates a thermal similarity index and evaluates the operational feasibility of new terrestrial analogs, detailing both their geological advantages and their irreversible physical limitations.

Use of Data from Space Agencies and Open Data Sources

Our project relies primarily on open databases to establish accurate baselines for parametric comparison. We use the following sources:

- NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO): We use the documented temperature ranges to establish the extreme parameters of the lunar South Pole (-250°C to 120°C) and the absence of atmospheric pressure in our comparison matrix.

- NASA InSight and Curiosity Rover (MEDA): To define the baseline for atmospheric pressure, temperature variation, and specific surface gravity for Gale Crater and landing sites on Mars.

- USGS / NASA Earth Observatory: We used technical documentation (such as the *Geologic Field Guide to S P Mountain and Its Lava Flow*, USGS 2021) to validate the geological criteria for basaltic analogs.

- European Space Agency (ESA) and DLR: To structure our matrix for characterizing controlled environments, we used technical reports from the LUNA analog facility in Cologne, Germany.

- Open-Meteo API (Earth Open Data): We integrated this API to extract, in real time, historical weather data (maximum and minimum temperatures and pressures from the past year) for the exact terrestrial locations queried by the user.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Disclosure)

We declare the responsible use of Generative Artificial Intelligence tools during the development phase of this project. AI assistants (LLMs) were used to support:

- Accelerating the structuring and debugging of Python source code (Streamlit and Pandas frameworks).

- Resolving deployment issues in cloud environments (Google Colab and GitHub Codespaces via tunnels).

- Optimizing the structure and technical writing of our documentation.

It should be noted that the conceptualization of the parametric comparison algorithm, the research and curated selection of scientific databases, and the technical evaluation of geological analogs were designed and directed entirely by the team’s human expertise.
